story_type: old munitions found off a beach, Navy divers destroy them offshore
hook: Old bombs, sitting in the water off a Hawaii beach.
narration: The Navy blew these up just four hundred yards off a Hawaii beach.
A citizen had reported possible unexploded ordnance in the water off Lanikai Beach.
They were likely World War Two era munitions, dropped during military training exercises.
Five members of a Navy explosive ordnance disposal team took a Zodiac raft out to the spot.
They brought eight smaller pieces to shore and lined them up, side by side.
Two more still had visible fuses, so those stayed out in the water.
Old munitions that have sat for decades can be unpredictable, so teams often destroy the worst ones right where they lie.
[short pause] With three fire in the hole warnings, the team set off C-4 charges attached to the two.
outcome: The charges went off, and water shot into the air four hundred yards offshore.
title: Old bombs found off a Hawaii beach
description:
On April 27, 2020, a Navy explosive ordnance disposal team removed eight potential pieces of unexploded ordnance from the water off Lanikai Beach in Kailua, Hawaii, and destroyed two more with a controlled detonation offshore.

Footage: U.S. Navy video by Petty Officer 2nd Class Charles Oki, via DVIDS: https://www.dvidshub.net/video/750059/lanikai-beach-uxo-removal

extra_sources.excerpt: With three successive “fire-in-the-hole” warnings, LT Jordan Bethke of the U.S. Navy’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team (Detachment Mid-Pacific) set off C-4 explosives attached to two potential Unexploded Ordnance (UXO) off Lanikai Beach this afternoon.
Water shot into the air during a brief explosion, 400 yards offshore; the explosion was likely caused from the C-4 and not necessarily from the UXO.

Five members of the team took a Zodiac raft out to where a citizen had reported possible unexploded ordnance in February. It is likely World War II era munitions dropped during military training exercises. Prior to the detonation of the two UXO, blown-up because fuses were still visible, the team brought eight smaller potential UXO to shore and lined them up, side-by-side.
